text: OK, proclamation. Lunar New Year Day. Whereas the traditional Chinese Lunar New Year celebration, also known as the Spring Festival, dates back as early as the 14th century BC, and whereas 2021 is the Year of the Ox, which is a symbol of wealth, prosperity, diligence, and perseverance, and those born during the Year of the Ox are said to be balanced, trustworthy, patient, and modest individuals, and whereas the Lunar New Year is celebrated uniquely in many different Asian countries, but regardless of the country, culture, religion, or ethnicity, the day is a time for family reunions, gatherings, reaffirming bonds, and reflection, and whereas the diverse Asian community in Renton is home for many Asian families that have been here for generations, as well as newer Asian immigrants, and whereas the city of Renton, with its rich demographic diversity, beautiful parks, friendly and prosperous businesses, many community services, and excellent schools has provided a welcoming environment for the Asian community to call Renton their home. Now, therefore, I, Armando Pavoni, mayor of the city of Renton, do hereby proclaim February 22, 2021 to be Lunar New Year day in the city of Renton, and I encourage all members of the community to join me in this special observance, in witness whereof, I adhere unto, set my hand, and cause the seal of the city of Renton to be affixed this 22nd day of February, 2021, signed Armando Pavoni, mayor of the city of Renton.

text: Greetings all. Can you all hear me? Yes? Okay. Yes. Yes. Good evening, Mr. Mayor, Council President Corman and members of the council. I appreciate staff's presentation and would just like to offer a few thoughts as we're a large land owner of the UC zone and are in the pre-development process for Southport's expansion. In general, we're supportive of working with staff to explore standards that diversify the UC zone retail base and ultimately support the city. There are a few considerations we're hoping the city will keep in mind as we go through the process. And the first being from our perspective, retail square footage is an artificial metric as evidenced by Fry's. Size is not what's contributing to the retail base. It's the spending. And when you layer in this sharp pivot towards e-commerce, there's no doubt that the complexion of retail is changing. Everything from big box to our small mom and pop spaces are struggling. And we're hoping to work towards development standards that choose a more flexible approach because oversupplying the market with a ton of retail space, in our opinion, is not the best way to provide fully integrated, smart retail spaces, which is what we need for the city to stay competitive. So that's first. Second, we're hoping that the city will approach from a macro lens. There are several hundred acres within this district, many ripe for redevelopment, and it's very challenging to prescribe these ecosystems on a site-by-site basis. It makes sense in our opinion to have sites that are primarily residential and are within a walkshed to concentrated retail spaces and employment. Every single use does not have to live on every single site. And if we're able to achieve porous ground level environments, we can create that there's there, which is vibrant and becomes the place where people really want to ultimately spend, which is what we're trying to achieve. And then lastly, we all know housing continues to be one of our region's biggest challenges. I sit on the city's housing action plan committee and having access to relatively affordable housing is something that SECO continues to promote. It's one of the best assets in Renton, especially when it comes to attracting large employers. And so meaningful residential projects, as exampled by the redevelopment of the Frye site is something our company is really excited and we've been sharing over the last couple of months since we became aware that there was a possible redevelopment and it's actually been received very well by potential office users who are wanting to provide options for their employees to live nearby. So with the large infusion of housing units, we believe there are significant economic benefits to be realized, including addressing the needs for the city's housing growth and diversification. And as I mentioned, attraction for large employers and search for housing for their employees, but probably the most relevant is large increases in retail spending for the area. The last thing we wanna see are projects like Frye's redevelopment or even our own expansion projects die on the vine because we're unable to get them underwritten to a standard that doesn't actually support the city. Big spaces don't always equate to smart spaces. So I appreciate being given the opportunity to testify tonight. And again, look forward to being part of a collaborative conversation in the near future. And I'm happy to answer any questions from staff or the council on behalf of SECO. But other than that, that's all I have tonight.

text: Good evening, my name is Paula Sardinas. I'm a resident of Federal Way, Washington. I'd like to thank the mayor, council president Foreman, and the honorable members of the council.
